extracted.intended_audience: authors and peer reviewers submitting to F1000Research
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on F1000Research's fully open, invited, post-publication peer review model for authors and reviewers, including what is reviewed, reviewer selection requirements, outcome categories, and criteria for passing and indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open, invited, formal peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Our peer review process is formal, invited, and fully open (meaning the reports are published alongside the article, along with reviewer names and affiliations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review reports, reviewer names and affiliations are published alongside the article — reviewer identities are not anonymous. Emphasises transparency and public availability of reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review takes place after the article has been published openly on the platform, so your research can start being read and used while expert reviewers assess it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles are published immediately with an 'Awaiting peer review' label; peer review happens on the live, published article rather than before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment focus: quality and validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to assess the quality and validity of the research – so null and negative studies are welcome on F1000Research, and won’t be reviewed any differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should focus on methodological and scientific validity rather than novelty or positive outcomes. Null/negative results are acceptable and assessed on the same criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article type eligibility for peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: F1000Research publishes a range of research outputs, which are all peer-reviewed except for Editorials, Posters, Slides, and Documents. Our other article types (such as Research Articles, Software Tool Articles, and Data Notes) undergo the same open, post-publication peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should confirm their article type; some formats are explicitly excluded from peer review (Editorials, Posters, Slides, Documents) while Research Articles, Software Tool Articles, Data Notes, etc., are peer-reviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review outcome categories and meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Status labels: 'Awaiting peer review' (applied immediately on publication), 'Approved' (the reviewer has asked for a few small changes, or no changes at all), 'Approved with reservations' (the reviewer believes the article has academic merit, but requires a number of small changes, or significant revisions), and 'Not approved' (the reviewer considers the article to have fundamental flaws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome labels are updated as reviews are published. 'Not approved' does not remove the article; authors are strongly encouraged to publish a revised version addressing specific concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for passing peer review and indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: An article passes peer review with two 'Approved' ratings, or one 'Approved' and two 'Approved with reservations', and will be included in PubMed, Scopus, and other major indexes, along with its review reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numeric thresholds determine when an article is considered to have 'passed' peer review and is eligible for inclusion in major indexing services; authors should aim to secure the required mix of reviewer ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-suggested reviewer requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Before publication, you must suggest at least five potential reviewers who meet our basic criteria (and must continue to suggest names until at least two peer review reports have been published).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are required to provide a minimum of five suggested reviewers up front and must keep suggesting additional names if necessary until at least two peer review reports are published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer identification and selection tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical advice: use your knowledge of the field to identify possible reviewers at relevant institutions; try the Reviewer Finder Tool; look at your references — authors of cited papers could be well-placed to review for you; explore academic databases like PubMed or Scopus for recent articles with relevant keywords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical strategies for compiling a list of suitable, expert reviewers, including use of publisher tools, citation lists, and database searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity considerations for suggested reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s important to think about the diversity of your suggested peer reviewers. Are they from different institutions? Are they from different countries? Is there a good gender balance? If the five names you provide aren’t diverse enough, we might ask you for more suggestions of potential reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for institutional, geographic, and gender diversity among suggested reviewers; the Editorial team may request additional or more diverse suggestions if the initial list is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial support for reviewer recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: If you struggle to find reviewers for your research, our Editorial team are there to support you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors who cannot identify suitable reviewers should contact the Editorial team for assistance; the team can help locate reviewers and facilitate the review process.
